title: Bhrigu, Varuna and the chant for two
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hook: a father won't hand his son the answer, and a chant counts exactly two
carry: brahman isn't handed down; teacher and student seek it
tomorrow: is the sound of a chant enough, or do you need the meaning?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants reached prachodayat: may he stir, a king's prayer for a lit mind. Now Priya needs a chant for the stage. The one she finds starts with a father and a son.

In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a young man named Bhrigu goes to his father, the god Varuna, and says: sir, teach me Brahman, the ultimate reality. Varuna doesn't give him the answer. He gives him a pointer: that from which all beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return. Seek to know that, through tapas, discipline. Bhrigu works, and comes back sure: it's food; everything lives by food. Varuna sends him back. Next time it's breath. Then mind. Then understanding. Each time, back he goes. At last Bhrigu sees it for himself: bliss. All beings are born from bliss, live by it, and return into it. The father never told him; he stayed his teacher the whole way.

The same Upanishad gives teacher and student a chant to say together before study: saha navavatu, saha nau bhunaktu, saha viryam karavavahai, tejasvi navadhitam astu, ma vidvishavahai. May it protect us two together, may it nourish us two, may we two make strength together, may our study be bright, may we two not turn against each other. The puzzle: Sanskrit has a set of forms for exactly two people, the dual, and every verb here uses it. The chant could have said we. It says us two. So why does the teacher pray at all? Many teachers explain it this way: the teacher doesn't own the truth and hand it down. Teacher and student both stand in front of Brahman, which neither of them made. Varuna didn't hand Bhrigu the answer; he sent him to see it, and stayed beside him. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, Brahman isn't handed down like a fact. A guru points, and the student has to see. Hindus call that bond guru and shishya, teacher and student, and the chant names it before one word is taught: we two are in this together; may we not fall out. Here's where it meets now. Priya picked this chant for the assembly. She'd planned to say it alone. Then Sam offered to read the English beside her, and the grammar settles it: this is a prayer built for two voices, two people learning the same thing side by side, neither one above the other.

segments.voice: Think of the next thing you'll learn today. Before you start, say saha navavatu, or its English, may we be protected together, with your fellow learners in mind. If you don't pray, name one person you learn alongside and send them a line of thanks. Then sit quietly until the time runs out.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: saha navavatu, a chant in the dual, where teacher and student pray as two.

chat.meaning: Saha navavatu is in the dual, for teacher and student together. Like Varuna with Bhrigu, the teacher doesn't own the truth; both seek Brahman.

notes: Peace chants, day 1 of 4 (1507–1510). Day 1769 (later this year) teaches saha navavatu by meaning (both, resentment in study); this day keeps to the dual grammar. Consider cross-reference when 1769 is next revised.

Grammar stated: nau as dual pronoun (nāv avatu by sandhi), avatu and bhunaktu as third singular imperatives ('may it'), karavāvahai and vidviṣāvahai as first person dual forms, adhītam 'what has been studied'. The subject 'it' is left unnamed (readers supply Brahman or 'he'). Confirm.
